Suppose the mixed-coordinate disintegration and local saddle estimates give the preceding expansion, with scalar remainder $O(qE_*^Ce^{\\zeta E_*^2}/N)$ at each actual mixed mesh point. Suppose centered-cell quadrature for the smooth leading terms costs $O(1/n)$ times the signed kernel envelope. Then, with the common normalization by $Z_*$, $$\\mathbb E_{\\rm Haar}\\left\\|\n Z_*^{-1}\\int A(zz^T-C_o)A\\,d(p-g)_{\\rm tilted}\n \\right\\|_{\\rm HS}^2\\le Cnq^2/N.$$",

        "anchor": "stmt-prof-endpoint-scalar",
        "exact_quote": "Let $P$ have finite second moment, put $q=\\mathbb E_P\\tanh^2 y$, $b=1-q$, and $a=\\mathbb E_P[(y-d)\\tanh y]$. For $\\nu>0$ with $\\nu\\ge q$, $$D(P\\Vert N(d,\\nu))\\ge\\frac{(a-\\nu b)^2}{2\\nu(\\nu+q)}.$$ Equality holds exactly when $P=N(d,\\nu)$. At every observation time $s>0$ the consistent equality law, with $d=s+\\mathbb E_P\\tanh y$ and $\\nu=s+q$, is uniquely $N(v_*(s),v_*(s))$, where $$v_*(s)=s+\\mathbb E_{N(v_*(s),v_*(s))}\\tanh y.$$ On compact positive time intervals this curve is continuous and its $q$ is bounded away from zero. The scalar integral and rate conclusions of Lemma 5.4(i), (ii), and (iv) of (OpenAI 2026a) [[AcceptedGap](#ref-AcceptedGap)] therefore hold at $j=1$ on such intervals. In particular, outside any fixed neighborhood of the equality curve, the smoothed scalar integral has strictly negative rate for sufficiently small smoothing variance.",
        "source_id": "PM-227.8"
      },
      "evidence": [
        {
          "anchor": "stmt-prof-endpoint-scalar",
          "exact_quote": "Let $P$ have finite second moment, put $q=\\mathbb E_P\\tanh^2 y$, $b=1-q$, and $a=\\mathbb E_P[(y-d)\\tanh y]$. At every observation time $s>0$ the consistent equality law, with $d=s+\\mathbb E_P\\tanh y$ and $\\nu=s+q$, is uniquely $N(v_*(s),v_*(s))$, where $$v_*(s)=s+\\mathbb E_{N(v_*(s),v_*(s))}\\tanh y.$$ On compact positive time intervals this curve is continuous and its $q$ is bounded away from zero. The scalar integral and rate conclusions of Lemma 5.4(i), (ii), and (iv) of (OpenAI 2026a) [[AcceptedGap](#ref-AcceptedGap)] therefore hold at $j=1$ on such intervals. Without the stability hypothesis, put $$Q_\\delta(h)=\\sup_{\\|F_h(y)\\|\\le\\delta\\sqrt n}q(y),$$ with an empty supremum equal to zero.         "anchor": "stmt-prof-terminal-extension",
        "exact_quote": "There are fixed $T,C,c>0$ and disorder events of ordinary probability at least $1-e^{-cn}$ with the following property. For every matrix in these events, let $X$ have any probability law on the cube, possibly depending on the matrix, and let the observation noises be independent of $X$. Set $h_T=TX+\\sqrt T\\,g$. The reference Gibbs law $\\mu_{h_T}$ has unscaled gap at least $1/2$ except with probability $e^{-cn}$.*\n\n*On the original spectral event choose a fixed $c_+$ such that $R=J+c_+I\\succeq0$. For one further time unit add observations with drift $RX$ and covariance rate $R$, obtaining $h_{T+\\lambda}$. Define the reference laws $$\\mu_{h,\\lambda}(x)\\ \\propto\\\n \\exp\\left(\\frac{1-\\lambda}{2}x^{\\mathsf T}J^\\circ x\n                         +h^{\\mathsf T}x\\right),\n \\qquad 0\\le\\lambda\\le1.$$ The covariance and inverse unscaled gap of $\\mu_{h_{T+\\lambda},\\lambda}$ are bounded by $C$, simultaneously in $\\lambda$, outside an event of conditional probability $e^{-cn}$, uniformly over the law generating $X$. At $\\lambda=1$ the reference law is product. These reference laws are the posteriors of the original Gibbs prior evaluated at the observations; no assertion about the posterior of the arbitrary law generating $X$ is made.",

      "conclusion": {
        "anchor": "stmt-cap-static-comparison",
        "exact_quote": "Fix a field radius $R<\\infty$, an error tolerance $\\eta>0$, and a geometric ratio in $(0,1)$. The statement remains valid for any fixed finite collection of auxiliary geometric cap lists. The zero-field concentration and density estimates used in the proof also allow bounded scalar modifications of the cap interaction whose spherical saddle gaps remain comparable to $p^2$.",

      },

          "anchor": "stmt-cap-static-comparison",
          "exact_quote": "Fix a field radius $R<\\infty$, an error tolerance $\\eta>0$, and a geometric ratio in $(0,1)$. There is a sufficiently small upper scale $p_0>0$ such that, with probability tending to one, simultaneously over a geometric list of caps $p\\le p_0$ with $np^3\\ge c\\sqrt{\\log n}$ and all $h\\in P_p\\mathbb R^n$ satisfying $\\|h\\|\\le R p^2 M_p$, one has $$\\label{cap:static-values}\n |\\log Z_p(h)-\\log Z_p^{\\rm sp}(h)|\\le \\eta k_p,\\qquad\n \\|P_p m_p(h)-a_p(h)\\|\\le \\eta M_p,\n \\qquad m_p(h)=\\nabla\\log Z_p(h).$$ The projected norm tails proved above hold, with a decreased positive exponential constant, under these cube posteriors and under the uncapped zero-field cube posterior. The statement remains valid for any fixed finite collection of auxiliary geometric cap lists. The zero-field concentration and density estimates used in the proof also allow bounded scalar modifications of the cap interaction whose spherical saddle gaps remain comparable to $p^2$.",

      "conclusion": {
        "anchor": "stmt-cap-curvature-induction",
        "exact_quote": "Fix a bounded child field range for the one-off evaluation conclusion below. There are a sufficiently large absolute $K_0$ and a sufficiently small ratio $\\gamma>0$ with the following property. Choose $\\sigma$ as a sufficiently high fixed power of $\\gamma$, and then choose $\\delta$ as a still higher fixed power, allowing these tolerances to depend on the prescribed field range. Let a parent potential at scale $p$ be intrinsic to the capped data, satisfy the value and gradient comparisons above, and satisfy <a href=\"#cap:invariant\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"cap:invariant\">[cap:invariant]</a> at all fields in <a href=\"#cap:annulus\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"cap:annulus\">[cap:annulus]</a>. Use the semiconcave extension just described when forming an auxiliary child potential. For a true parent, retain the true child potential. Condition on the parent data and used auxiliary randomness $\\mathscr F_p$ described below, on which these hypotheses and the $\\mathscr F_p$-measurable parent-level conclusions of the static comparison hold, including the projected posterior tail and moment bounds for this capped parent. The separate $o(1)$ failure probability used to obtain these parent conclusions remains outside the conditional estimate below. Then, uniformly over such parent data, the probability over the unused Haar refinement $O$ that <a href=\"#cap:invariant\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"cap:invariant\">[cap:invariant]</a> fails at $c=\\gamma p$ anywhere on the child annulus is at most $$C e^{-a k_p}+C e^{-a' k_c}$$ for fixed positive $a,a'$. The same inequalities hold with strict slack on the complementary event. These failure probabilities are summable over the geometric cap list.*\n\n*At intermediate ratios $c/p\\in[\\gamma,1)$, if the frozen parameter stays inside the agreement domain with fixed slack, the transverse error and mixed block tend to zero with the parent errors, the total scaled Hessian is bounded, and the radial deficit is at least $0.26$. The same deterministic evaluation bounds hold for $c/p\\in[\\gamma^2,\\gamma]$ under this interior-parameter condition. For a true parent and the prescribed bounded child field range there is also a sufficiently small fixed evaluation-ratio interval on which the upper child curvature is at most $C/c^2$, with $C$ depending only on that field range. This last evaluation uses supports centered at the frozen parameter, constructed at the end of the proof. All statements are uniform down to $np^3\\asymp\\sqrt{\\log n}$.",

        "anchor": "stmt-cap-frozen-evaluation-support",
        "exact_quote": "Fix a child field radius $R$ before choosing the curvature and comparison tolerances. Suppose a true parent at scale $p$ satisfies the invariant and the static comparisons. There is a fixed $b_1>0$, depending on $R,\\sigma$, such that the following holds for every $x\\in[\\gamma b_1,b_1]$, $c=xp$, and $h\\in H_c$ with $\\|h\\|\\le R c^2M_c$. Put $\\alpha=\\alpha_c(h)$. With sufficiently small fixed tolerances, there is an upper-semiconcave extension agreeing with the true parent on a neighborhood of the frozen typical length sphere. Its convolution has a strict margin, and its terminal mean and covariance differ from those of the true transition by exponentially small errors in the corresponding scaled units. Consequently, $$\\label{cap:ball-evaluation-bound}\n K_c(h)\\preceq C(R)c^{-2}I_{H_c},$$ where $C(R)$ is independent of the chosen ratios and sharp curvature tolerances. The construction and estimates are uniform on the indicated fixed ratio interval, with $n$ taken large after those choices.",

        "exact_quote": "Fix $0<\\beta<1$, an operator-norm bound for $J_*$, and fixed positive parameters in <a href=\"#cap:stability-test\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"cap:stability-test\">[cap:stability-test]</a>, with $j(1+\\eta)^2<1$. On the fixed-length matrix-word events described below, every field satisfying <a href=\"#cap:stability-test\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"cap:stability-test\">[cap:stability-test]</a> has a unique root $y_*$ of $F_h$. If $m_* =\\tanh y_*$ and $$\\mu_h(x)\\propto\\exp\\{x^{\\mathsf T}J_*x/2+h^{\\mathsf T}x\\},\n \\qquad\n \\mathcal D_h(f)=\\sum_i\\mathbb E_{\\mu_h}\n                 \\operatorname{Var}(f\\mid x_{\\ne i}),$$ then $$\\label{cap:classical-mean-covariance}\n \\|\\mathbb E_{\\mu_h}x-m_*\\|\\le C,\n \\qquad \\|\\operatorname{Cov}_{\\mu_h}(x)\\|\\le C.$$ For every sufficiently small fixed $\\epsilon>0$, every real $f$ with $N=\\mathbb E_{\\mu_h}f^2>0$, and $\\nu=f^2\\mu_h/N$, $$\\label{cap:square-reweighting}\n |\\mathbb E_\\nu x-m_*|_n\n \\le C\\epsilon+\\frac{C_\\epsilon}{\\sqrt n}\n                    \\left(1+\\frac{\\mathcal D_h(f)}{N}\\right).$$ The event and constants are independent of $h$ and $f$ under the stated diagnostics and stability parameters. The required word length is finite and may depend on $\\epsilon$.*\n\n*The same conclusions hold at $j=1$ if, in addition, every approximate root in the residual region has $q\\ge q_{\\min}>0$, and the inverse-word event is restricted to the diagonal class specified in Lemma <a href=\"#cap:restricted-words\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"cap:restricted-words\">38</a>.         "exact_quote": "Assume the preceding spectral and noise diagnostics, the zero-field approximate-root exclusion in Lemma <a href=\"#cap:endpoint-stability\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"cap:endpoint-stability\">39</a>, the field representation <a href=\"#cap:boundary-field\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"cap:boundary-field\">[cap:boundary-field]</a>, and $|P_t^Wh|_n\\ge ct^{5/4}$. For a starting direction $v$, let $v_s$ solve $$\\label{cap:linear-flow}\n dv_s=dB_s\\,K_s v_s=G_sK_sv_s\\,ds.$$ Then $$e_{s_0}^{\\mathsf T}v\n      =\\mathbb E[e_{s_1}^{\\mathsf T}v_{s_1}\\mid h_{s_0}],$$ whenever the indicated polynomial moments are finite. The same identity holds by approximation for the extensions used here.",

        "anchor": "stmt-cap-layer-lemma",
        "exact_quote": "Let $\\eta$ be a strictly positive probability measure on a finite state space, let $\\mathcal E$ be a reversible Markov Dirichlet form, and suppose $\\min_x\\eta(x)\\ge e^{-M}$, with $M\\ge\\log2$. Suppose that, for some $A>0$, $$\\mathcal E(g)\\ge A\\eta[g^2]\\log\\frac1{\\eta[g^2]}$$ for every $0\\le g\\le1$ supported on a set of measure at most $1/2$ and satisfying $$D\\!\\left(\\frac{g^2\\eta}{\\eta[g^2]}\\middle\\Vert\\eta\\right)\n \\ge\\frac12\\log\\frac1{\\eta[g^2]},\\qquad\n 0<\\log\\frac1{\\eta[g^2]}\\le M.$$ Then, with an absolute constant $C$, $$\\label{cap:layer-lsi}\n \\operatorname{Ent}_{\\eta}(f^2)\n \\le \\frac{C(1+\\log_+M)^2}{A}\\,\\mathcal E(f)\n \\qquad\\text{for every real-valued }f.$$",
        "source_id": "PM-227.8"
      },

        "anchor": "stmt-cap-observation-identities",
        "exact_quote": "Along the continuous portions of this path, $$\\begin{aligned}\n -\\dot H(s)\n &=\\tfrac12\\mathbb E_{Q_\\nu}\n       \\|m_{\\nu,s}-m_{\\mu,s}\\|_{G_s}^2,\n       \\label{cap:entropy-identity}\\\\\n \\mathbb E_{Q_\\nu}\n     \\frac{\\mathcal D_{\\mu_s}(f)}{N_s}\n &\\le\\frac{\\mathcal D_0(f)}N.\n       \\label{cap:energy-conditioning}\n\\end{aligned}$$ The continuous entropy-loss integral up to a stopping time, together with the information from preceding precision jumps, gives the relative entropy of the stopped observation laws. Moreover, for $v\\ge0$, $$\\label{cap:conditional-entropy-tail}\n Q_\\nu(l_s>L+v)\\le e^{-v},\\qquad\n Q_\\nu(E)\\le e^L Q_\\mu(E)$$ for every observation event $E$, including stopped-path events.",

    {
      "conclusion": {
        "anchor": "stmt-cap-lower-test",
        "exact_quote": "The static comparison also gives a direct, weaker-in-quantifiers route to the matching worst-start lower exponent. Fix $0<\\epsilon<1/3$ and take $p=n^{-1/3+\\epsilon}$. In the uncapped zero-field spherical model, $\\|P_pX\\|\\ge cM_p$ with probability tending to one. To see this, compare with the Gaussian of precision $2+\\xi p^2-J$. A spectral band with gaps comparable to $p^2$ already has this lower bound outside $e^{-ck_p}$. The lower norm-density estimate and the bounded density of the remaining coordinates transfer it through norm conditioning, when $\\xi>0$ is sufficiently small. Haar first moments and the zero-field second-moment comparison in Proposition <a href=\"#cap:static-comparison\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"cap:static-comparison\">33</a> transfer the conclusion to the cube with high Gibbs probability for typical disorder. Spin symmetry and $\\operatorname{rank}P_p\\le Cnp^3$ imply that some Euclidean unit vector $a$ has $$\\operatorname{Var}_\\mu(a^{\\mathsf T}X)\\ge c p^{-2},\n \\qquad\n \\mathcal D_0(a^{\\mathsf T}X)\n =\\sum_i a_i^2\\mu[\\operatorname{Var}(X_i\\mid X_{-i})]\\le1.$$ Thus the rate-one spectral gap is at most $Cp^2$. Testing a gap eigenfunction from a state where its absolute value is maximal gives $t_{\\rm mix}(1/4)\\ge c p^{-2}$; the discrete gap is smaller by $n$. Letting the fixed $\\epsilon$ decrease proves the same lower exponents. The realized-start statement and the bounds for every arbitrarily slowly diverging $M_n$ remain the separate conclusions of Theorem <a href=\"#thm:accepted-critical\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"thm:accepted-critical\">2</a>.",
        "source_id": "PM-227.8"
      },

<a id="pm-s2"></a>
## 2. Definitions, validity and bounds

- **Gaussian SK Gibbs law** ([source](#eq:gibbs-law)): Let $J^\circ$ be a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal and independent $J^\circ_{ij}\sim N(0,1/n)$ for $i<j$. On $\Omega_n=\{-1,1\}^n$, put $$\label{eq:gibbs-law} \mu_J(x)=Z_J^{-1}\exp\!\left(\frac12x^{\mathsf T}J^\circ x\right).$$ This is Gaussian SK at inverse temperature one and zero external field. Write $Q_i$ for conditional expectation under $\mu_J$ given $x_{-i}$, and set $$\label{eq:clock-conventions} \mathcal L_J=\sum_{i=1}^n(Q_i-I),\qquad P_J=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nQ_i,\qquad \mathcal D_J(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_J\!\left[\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_J}(f\mid x_{-i})\right].$$ Thus $\mathcal L_J=n(P_J-I)$, and a discrete attempt may leave the spin unchanged. Let $t_{\mathrm{mix},J}(\varepsilon)$ and $k_{\mathrm{mix},J}(\varepsilon)$ denote worst-start total-variation mixing times for $e^{t\mathcal L_J}$ and $P_J^k$, respectively. The default threshold is $1/4$.
- **Relaxation time and log-Sobolev inverse constant** ([source](#eq:relaxation-definition)): $$\begin{aligned} R_J&=\sup_{\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_J}(f)>0}\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_J}(f)}{\mathcal D_J(f)}, \label{eq:relaxation-definition}\\ C_{\mathrm{LS},J}&=\sup_{\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mu_J}(f^2)>0} \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mu_J}(f^2)}{\mathcal D_J(f)}, \label{eq:lsi-definition} \end{aligned}$$ where $\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(g)=\mu(g\log g)-\mu(g)\log\mu(g)$ for $g\ge0$. Both constants use the unscaled sum of heat-bath conditional variances. Thus $R_J$ is the relaxation time for the rate-one-per-site generator; for one attempted update the relaxation time is $nR_J$. The conditional variance weights in $\mathcal D_J$ are retained in every comparison below.
- **Completed GOE matrix** ([source](#sec:model)): Adjoin independent $J_{ii}\sim N(0,2/n)$ to $J^\circ$ and call the completed matrix $J$.
- **Heat-bath Dirichlet form** ([source](#sec:model)): For a full-support law $\nu$ on $\Omega_n$, we write $$\mathcal D_\nu(f)=\sum_i\nu\!\left[\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\nu(f\mid X_{-i})\right].$$
- **Worst-start mixing times** ([source](#sec:introduction)): Let $t_{\mathrm{mix},J}(\varepsilon)$ and $k_{\mathrm{mix},J}(\varepsilon)$ denote worst-start total-variation mixing times for $e^{t\mathcal L_J}$ and $P_J^k$, respectively.
- **Cap precision** ([source](#pm-h-16)): At scale $p$, observe with precision $B_p=(p^2-d)_+$ and write $J_p=J-B_p$.
- **Radial deficit** ([source](#pm-h-16)): This negative radial correction is the *radial deficit*.
- **Entropy-production constant** ([source](#pm-h-113)): This is the inverse constant for the logarithmic entropy-production inequality.

<a id="pm-s3"></a>
## 3. Proof roadmap

- **s-spectral-edge** [claim](#stmt-prof-lem-spectrum) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-lem-spectrum): Tridiagonal representation, resolvent walk expansions, Hermite equation for the deterministic trace -> edge resolvent and counting estimates
- **s-density-at-mean** [claim](#stmt-prof-quadratic-mean-density) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-quadratic-mean-density): Case analysis on subsequences with Fourier inversion -> lower density bound at the mean
- **s-spherical-normalization** [claim](#stmt-prof-lem-spherical-z) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-lem-spherical-z): Gaussian shell formula and concavity of log determinant -> two-sided zero-field spherical normalization
- **s-spherical-observation** [claim](#stmt-prof-lem-spherical-observation) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-lem-spherical-observation): Test the spherical root equation at trial points with Gaussian exponentiation -> concentration of root parameter and mean norm
- **s-unconstrained-orbit** [claim](#stmt-prof-prop-unconstrained) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-prop-unconstrained): Replica integrals, Paley-Zygmund, controlled rotational Brownian motion with reflection -> cube versus sphere partition comparison on orbits
- **s-edge-window** [claim](#stmt-prof-prop-polylog) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-prop-polylog): Second-moment comparison with signed alternating sum and Fourier inversion -> partition ratio near one and moment comparison
- **s-root-count** [claim](#stmt-prof-root-count) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-root-count): Kac-Rice area formula with Gaussian conditioning -> exact counting density
- **s-determinant-bound** [claim](#stmt-prof-determinant-square) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-determinant-square): Finite-rank reduction and exterior-variable second moment -> polynomial determinant second moment
- **s-scalar-diagnostics** [claim](#stmt-prof-scalar-diagnostics) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-scalar-diagnostics): Scalar variational comparison, moment expansion, phase dispersion -> retained scalar parameters and moments
- **s-conditioned-precision** [claim](#stmt-prof-conditioned-precision) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-conditioned-precision): Haar concentration, Schur complements, interlacing -> precision lower bounds and projection variances
- **s-unique-root** [claim](#stmt-prof-unique-root) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-unique-root): Positive Jacobian and degree-one homotopy -> regular unique root on retained event
- **s-trace-three-densities** [claim](#stmt-prof-trace-from-three-densities) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-trace-from-three-densities): Exponential tilting of the squared length and Fourier bounds -> trace location within one fluctuation
- **s-angular-kernel** [claim](#stmt-prof-common-angular-kernel) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-common-angular-kernel): Gram invariants and Haar disintegration in one chart -> common angular kernel and mixed measures
- **s-mixed-transfer** [claim](#stmt-prof-mixed-coordinate-transfer) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-mixed-coordinate-transfer): Separate remainder bounds and quadrature then signed sum -> common-volume cancellation
- **s-signed-gaussian-kernel** [claim](#stmt-prof-gaussian-signed-kernel) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-gaussian-signed-kernel): Wick expansion under complex Fourier tilt with parity comparison -> signed density bounds and odd-part gain
- **s-surviving-coefficients** [claim](#stmt-prof-surviving-coefficients) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-surviving-coefficients): Cumulant computation at zero projection and alternating cancellation -> explicit surviving odd term
- **s-weighted-transfer** [claim](#stmt-prof-weighted-kernel-transfer) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-weighted-kernel-transfer): Account for scalar remainders, odd term and quadrature -> weighted second-moment comparison
- **s-median-covariance** [claim](#stmt-prof-median-covariance) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-median-covariance): Three priors with projection cuts, signed pair comparison, Markov exclusion -> covariance and mean bounds on most orientations
- **s-compact-overlap** [claim](#stmt-prof-lem-compact-bridge) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-lem-compact-bridge): Annulus penalty for replica statistics with first-crossing selection -> overlap tails on compact intervals
- **s-conditional-variance** [claim](#stmt-prof-lem-conditional-variance) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-lem-conditional-variance): Likelihood transfer to Gaussian reference and Langevin telescoping -> weak Poincare inequality for one backward step
- **s-amplified-covariance** [claim](#stmt-prof-prop-amplified-covariance) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-prop-amplified-covariance): Backward induction with variance transfer and orbit reset -> sharp covariance down to logarithmic scale
- **s-bottom-covariance** [claim](#stmt-prof-prop-bottom-covariance) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-prop-bottom-covariance): Finite-replica expansion with label cancellation -> coarse covariance with high polynomial probability
- **s-endpoint-words** [claim](#stmt-prof-endpoint-words) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-endpoint-words): Gaussian comparison, loop equations, chaining -> simultaneous word diagnostics
- **s-endpoint-logdet** [claim](#stmt-prof-endpoint-logdet) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-endpoint-logdet): Path integration of the log determinant and concentration with a mesh -> restricted determinant bound
- **s-endpoint-scalar** [claim](#stmt-prof-endpoint-scalar) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-endpoint-scalar): Change of variables entropy bound and equality curve analysis -> scalar rate and equality curve
- **s-positive-stability** [claim](#stmt-prof-positive-stability) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-positive-stability): Conditional finite-rank matrix test and local-volume exclusion -> stable-field implication at positive times
- **s-endpoint-posterior** [claim](#stmt-prof-endpoint-posterior) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-endpoint-posterior): Residual recipes, selection cutoffs, finite-flip buffers -> covariance and mean transfer bounds
- **s-terminal-extension** [claim](#stmt-prof-terminal-extension) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-terminal-extension): Signed curvature inequality with sparse biased coordinates -> terminal gap and product endpoint
- **s-restricted-profile** [claim](#stmt-prof-restricted-profile) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-restricted-profile): Entropy retention in three ranges, Gronwall, product endpoint inequality -> support profile for bounded tests
- **s-uniform-profile** [claim](#stmt-prof-thm-profile) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prof-thm-profile): Dyadic layers and median decomposition -> uniform support profile and gap
- **s-static-cap** [claim](#stmt-cap-static-comparison) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-static-comparison): Replica Gram comparison, angular second moment, refinement from coarser cap -> cube versus sphere values and means on caps
- **s-curvature-step** [claim](#stmt-cap-curvature-induction) / [proof](#pm-h-75): Semiconcave extension, Brascamp-Lieb and Fisher bounds, Haar compression -> curvature invariant at the next cap
- **s-deterministic-evaluation** [claim](#stmt-cap-deterministic-evaluation) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-deterministic-evaluation): Reuse of the extension with convolution margin -> intermediate-scale bounds
- **s-frozen-evaluation** [claim](#stmt-cap-frozen-evaluation-support) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-frozen-evaluation-support): Supports centered at the frozen parameter -> ball curvature bound
- **s-restricted-words** [claim](#stmt-cap-restricted-words) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-restricted-words): Norm-trace margin in loop equations and chaining -> endpoint matrix diagnostics
- **s-classical-input** [claim](#stmt-cap-classical-input) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-restricted-words-2): Companion residual identities with restricted diagonal buffers -> posterior mean and covariance at the boundary
- **s-cap-endpoint-stability** [claim](#stmt-cap-endpoint-stability) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-endpoint-stability): Scalar rate, conditional matrix law, local volume -> stability along positive-time paths
- **s-boundary-noise** [claim](#stmt-cap-boundary-noise) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-boundary-noise): Frame comparison and Gaussian small-ball bound -> uniform noise diagnostics
- **s-tap-expansion** [claim](#stmt-cap-tap-expansion) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-tap-expansion): Clipped band localization, low-band cancellation, rank-one response -> boundary root, response and potential value
- **s-terminal-tests** [claim](#stmt-cap-marked-terminal-tests) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-marked-terminal-tests): Canonical Gaussian length tests transferred to cube posteriors by marked replicas -> terminal domain and length tests
- **s-auxiliary-initialization** [claim](#stmt-cap-auxiliary-initialization) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-auxiliary-initialization): Nested terminal regions, extension, Brascamp-Lieb and Fisher bounds -> auxiliary potential with invariant and bounded gradient error
- **s-gradient-transport** [claim](#stmt-cap-gradient-transport) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-gradient-transport): Ito formula along the observation with a linear flow -> error transport identity
- **s-gradient-contraction** [claim](#stmt-cap-gradient-contraction) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-gradient-contraction): Rank flow along the bridge and conditional Haar projection -> halved gradient discrepancy
- **s-remove-auxiliary** [claim](#stmt-cap-remove-auxiliary) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-remove-auxiliary): Lipschitz tilt with subgaussian moments -> true potential satisfies invariant
- **s-true-curvature** [claim](#stmt-cap-true-curvature) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-true-curvature): Iterate the cap step down to the cutoff and evaluate at other ratios -> uniform curvature of true cap potentials
- **s-layer-lemma** [claim](#stmt-cap-layer-lemma) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-layer-lemma): Equal-height layers, capacity bound, dyadic sum, entropy shift -> log-Sobolev from bounded-test energy bound
- **s-observation-identities** [claim](#stmt-cap-observation-identities) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-observation-identities): Likelihood ratio, chain rule for relative entropy, conditional variance -> entropy and energy identities
- **s-critical-lsi** [claim](#stmt-cap-thm-lsi) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cap-thm-lsi): Entropy retention along cap path, product endpoint estimate, stopped-path contradiction for large entropy -> critical log-Sobolev inequality
- **s-linear-lower-test** [claim](#stmt-cap-lower-test) / [proof](#stmt-cap-lower-test): Linear test from spherical comparison -> direct lower exponent for the gap
- **s-profile-to-mixing** [claim](#stmt-lem-profile-to-mixing) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-profile-to-mixing): Density truncation, squared-norm decay, Poincare tail -> mixing time bounds in both clocks
- **s-entropy-production** [claim](#stmt-cor-entropy-production) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cor-entropy-production): Two-point inequality and small-perturbation expansion -> entropy-production exponent
- **s-companion-lower-bounds** [claim](#stmt-thm-accepted-critical) / [proof](#stmt-thm-accepted-critical): Imported from companion -> realized-start and linear lower bounds
- **s-main-theorem** [claim](#stmt-thm-main) / [proof](#pm-h-112): Combine upper bounds through both routes with companion lower bounds -> critical exponents

<a id="pm-s4"></a>
## 4. Engineering Triptych

### Panel 1 - epistemic contract

- **inv-critical-mixing-exponents**: At the critical zero-field Gaussian SK model, in probability over the disorder, the worst-start mixing times, the relaxation time and the classical logarithmic Sobolev constant all have exponent slack o(1): continuous time and relaxation scale as n^{2/3+o(1)}, attempted updates as n^{5/3+o(1)}. The statement is an asymptotic exponent statement, not a bound with a leading constant.
- **inv-realized-start-lower-bound**: For deterministic time sequences below the critical scale, a realized equilibrium start stays at total-variation distance above the threshold from equilibrium with probability tending to one; this lower bound is imported from the companion work.
- **inv-uniform-support-profile**: On one disorder event of probability tending to one, the heat-bath Dirichlet form of every nonzero real function with support mass at most one half is bounded below by a power of n times the log inverse support mass times its squared norm, with exponent slack omega.
- **inv-critical-log-sobolev**: With probability tending to one over the Gaussian couplings, the entropy of the square of every real function is bounded by n^{2/3+rho} times the unscaled heat-bath Dirichlet form of that function.

### Panel 2 - negative knowledge

- **anti-other-temperature**: Reusing the critical mixing exponent for a different inverse temperature, either above or below the critical one. -> The exponent is proved only at the critical point; neighbouring temperatures have different mixing behaviour and the source says limits from the subcritical side give no bound at the endpoint.
- **anti-external-field**: Applying the bounds to a model with a nonzero external field. -> The proofs use zero-field symmetry and the orthogonal invariance of the completed matrix; no statement is made with a field.
- **anti-cutoff-constant**: Reading the exponent as a sharp cutoff location, cutoff window or leading constant for runtime planning. -> The theorem only fixes the exponent up to n^{o(1)} slack, so any constant-factor schedule is unsupported.
- **anti-linear-to-full**: Transferring the arbitrary-diverging-factor bounds for linear observables to the full relaxation or logarithmic Sobolev constants. -> The upper estimates for the full constants carry fixed positive exponent slack, not an arbitrary diverging factor.

### Panel 3 - reference implementation and oracle

Applicability: `not_applicable`. The main results are asymptotic exponent statements holding in probability over random Gaussian disorder, established by probabilistic and spectral arguments with unspecified constants and slack; the source states no finite procedure with explicit steps and computable output whose correctness could be executed and checked by an independent oracle.

This is a scheduling heuristic, not a constructive algorithm. |
| tools | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | No tool, checker or interface is constructed. The only operational convention in the paper is the default total-variation threshold used to define the mixing times. |

| machine_learning | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The paper treats an equilibrium sampling problem for a spin glass and trains nothing. The logarithmic Sobolev inequality is relevant to the sampler's speed, not to learning guarantees. |
| optimisation_operations_research | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The result concerns sampling from a Gibbs law, not minimizing an objective. No optimization algorithm or approximation guarantee is stated. |
| distributed_systems | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | Updates are single-site on one machine in the model; there is no communication, consensus or fault model. Parallel or asynchronous updates are not analyzed. |
| other | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | No further application domain is supported by the text. Its value is mathematical, namely the sharp exponent at the critical temperature. |

## 6. Applicability limits and search

- **lim-critical-zero-field-only** (hypothesis): The exponents are proved only for the Gaussian SK model at inverse temperature one with zero external field. Other temperatures or nonzero fields are outside the statement. Blocked use: ['Reusing the exponents at an inverse temperature different from one', 'Applying the bounds to a Hamiltonian with a nonzero external field']
- **lim-exponent-slack-only** (formal_scope): Each exponent statement means only that, for every fixed positive tolerance, the quantity lies between powers of n with that tolerance. It carries no explicit constants, so it is asymptotic and has no finite-n guarantee. Blocked use: ['Reading n^{2/3+o(1)} as a bound with a known prefactor at a given n', 'Quoting a numeric step budget derived from the exponent']
- **lim-no-cutoff-claim** (formal_scope): The paper determines the mixing exponent only. It asserts neither a cutoff, nor a cutoff window, nor a leading constant. Blocked use: ['Treating the exponent as a sharp transition time', 'Using the result to locate a cutoff window']
- **lim-quantifier-gap-linear-vs-full** (formal_scope): The arbitrary-diverging-factor bounds hold only for the covariance norm and the linear Rayleigh quotient. The upper bounds for the full relaxation and log-Sobolev constants carry fixed positive exponent slack. Blocked use: ['Transferring the arbitrary diverging slack from linear observables to the full constants', 'Using linear-observable relaxation as a proxy for worst-start total-variation mixing']
- **lim-realized-start-imported** (formal_scope): The realized-equilibrium-start lower bound is imported from the companion theorems and holds for deterministic time sequences below the critical scale. It is not proved in this paper. Blocked use: ['Citing it as a result proved here', 'Applying it to random or data-dependent time sequences']
- **lim-no-subcritical-limit** (hypothesis): Fixed-subcritical results do not yield a bound at the critical endpoint by taking a limit of the inverse temperature. Blocked use: ['Deriving the critical exponent by letting beta tend to one in subcritical gap or mixing theorems']
- **lim-stable-field-not-all-fields** (hypothesis): The stable-field theorem is along ordinary Gaussian observations of a zero-field Gibbs sample. It is not a theorem for every field. Blocked use: ['Using whole-region stability for arbitrary external fields', 'Applying the posterior estimates outside the retained field event']
- **lim-single-path-covariance** (edge_case): A covariance estimate on one random observation path is not an all-tilts stability theorem. The classical log-Sobolev argument needs its own entropy and layer argument. Blocked use: ['Using path-wise covariance bounds as a uniform bound over all tilts']
- **lim-planted-spectral-event** (edge_case): The spectral event is imposed under ordinary disorder, and the planted probability of the event need not be large. Planted estimates are returned to ordinary disorder with the stated probability cost. Blocked use: ['Assuming the spectral event has large planted probability', 'Applying planted bounds without the transfer to ordinary disorder']
- **lim-restricted-diagonal-class** (hypothesis): The determinant and word diagnostics at the endpoint hold only for diagonal compressions in the restricted class with a strict norm-trace margin. Arbitrary positive contractions chosen after the matrix are excluded. Blocked use: ['Extending the determinant bound to contractions chosen adaptively from the matrix']
- **lim-unscaled-dirichlet-form** (hypothesis): The constants use the unscaled sum of heat-bath conditional variances. Other normalizations of the form or of the clock change the constants by factors such as n. Blocked use: ['Comparing the constants with results stated for a rescaled Dirichlet form without conversion']
- **lim-nonconstructive-selection** (nonconstructive): The macroscopic-entropy range argues along a diagonally selected sequence of violating functions. This is a selection-and-contradiction argument, not a constructive procedure. Blocked use: ['Extracting an algorithm or explicit constants from this step']

<a id="pm-s7"></a>
## 7. Complete mathematical paper


At the critical inverse temperature <i>β</i> = 1, we determine the worst-start total-variation mixing exponent for single-site heat-bath dynamics in the zero-field Gaussian Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model. The mixing time is $`n^{2/3+o(1)}`$ when every site has rate one, or $`n^{5/3+o(1)}`$ attempted uniform-site updates, in probability over the disorder.

<a id="sec:introduction"></a>
### Introduction

We determine the mixing exponent of single-site heat-bath dynamics at the critical temperature of the zero-field Gaussian Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model. Starting from the worst configuration, the dynamics mixes in time $n^{2/3+o(1)}$ when each site has rate one, or after $n^{5/3+o(1)}$ attempted uniform-site updates. The same per-site exponent governs the relaxation time and the inverse classical logarithmic Sobolev constant.

At criticality, equilibrium fluctuations are much larger than for independent spins. An upper mixing bound must hold from every initial configuration, while the functional bounds must hold for every test function. We obtain these uniform controls in two ways. The first relates a function’s heat-bath energy to the mass of its support. The second proves a classical logarithmic Sobolev inequality. Each argument has its own initialization and entropy estimates.

<a id="eq:gibbs-law"></a>
Let $J^\circ$ be a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal and independent $J^\circ_{ij}\sim N(0,1/n)$ for $i<j$. On $\Omega_n=\{-1,1\}^n$, put $$\label{eq:gibbs-law}
 \mu_J(x)=Z_J^{-1}\exp\!\left(\frac12x^{\mathsf T}J^\circ x\right).$$ This is Gaussian SK at inverse temperature one and zero external field. Write $Q_i$ for conditional expectation under $\mu_J$ given $x_{-i}$, and set <a id="eq:clock-conventions"></a>$$\label{eq:clock-conventions}
 \mathcal L_J=\sum_{i=1}^n(Q_i-I),\qquad
 P_J=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nQ_i,\qquad
 \mathcal D_J(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_J\!\left[\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_J}(f\mid x_{-i})\right].$$ Thus $\mathcal L_J=n(P_J-I)$, and a discrete attempt may leave the spin unchanged. Let $t_{\mathrm{mix},J}(\varepsilon)$ and $k_{\mathrm{mix},J}(\varepsilon)$ denote worst-start total-variation mixing times for $e^{t\mathcal L_J}$ and $P_J^k$, respectively. The default threshold is $1/4$.

Define the relaxation time and the classical logarithmic Sobolev inverse constant by <a id="eq:relaxation-definition"></a><a id="eq:lsi-definition"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 R_J&=\sup_{\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_J}(f)>0}\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_J}(f)}{\mathcal D_J(f)},
 \label{eq:relaxation-definition}\\
 C_{\mathrm{LS},J}&=\sup_{\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mu_J}(f^2)>0}
               \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mu_J}(f^2)}{\mathcal D_J(f)},
 \label{eq:lsi-definition}
\end{aligned}$$ where $\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(g)=\mu(g\log g)-\mu(g)\log\mu(g)$ for $g\ge0$. Both constants use the unscaled sum of heat-bath conditional variances. Thus $R_J$ is the relaxation time for the rate-one-per-site generator; for one attempted update the relaxation time is $nR_J$. The conditional variance weights in $\mathcal D_J$ are retained in every comparison below.

<a id="stmt-thm-main"></a>
<div id="thm:main" class="theorem">

**Theorem 1** (Critical mixing and functional inequalities). *For every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, in probability over the Gaussian disorder, $$\begin{aligned}
 t_{\mathrm{mix},J}(\varepsilon)&=n^{2/3+o(1)},&
 k_{\mathrm{mix},J}(\varepsilon)&=n^{5/3+o(1)},\\
 R_J&=n^{2/3+o(1)},& C_{\mathrm{LS},J}&=n^{2/3+o(1)}.
\end{aligned}$$ In each expression, $X_n=n^{a+o(1)}$ means that for every fixed $\delta>0$, $\mathbb P\{n^{a-\delta}\le X_n\le n^{a+\delta}\}\to1$.*

</div>

The two functional constants describe complementary forms of relaxation. For every centered observable $f$, the spectral theorem gives $\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_J}(e^{t\mathcal L_J}f)\le e^{-2t/R_J}\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_J}(f)$, with equality for a slowest eigenfunction. The classical logarithmic Sobolev inequality supplies hypercontractive smoothing for arbitrary densities and implies the Poincaré inequality. [sec:dynamics](#sec:dynamics) derives the worst-start bounds from these controls. Let $\operatorname{KL}$ denote relative entropy. [cor:entropy-production](#cor:entropy-production) also gives the same per-site exponent for the inverse of the best rate $c$ such that $\operatorname{KL}(\nu e^{t\mathcal L_J}\Vert\mu_J)
\le e^{-ct}\operatorname{KL}(\nu\Vert\mu_J)$ for every initial probability law $\nu$ on the cube and every $t\ge0$.

The contribution of this paper is the upper bounds. To state precisely how they combine with the existing lower bounds, we record the critical companion’s realized-start and linear-observable theorems (OpenAI 2026b, Theorems 1.2 and 1.3) <a id="pm-cite-1"></a>[[AcceptedCritical](#ref-AcceptedCritical)]. Their quantifiers are stronger than fixed exponent bounds and will be retained throughout.

<a id="stmt-thm-accepted-critical"></a>
<div id="thm:accepted-critical" class="theorem">

**Theorem 2** (Realized equilibrium starts and linear observables). *For every deterministic sequence $t_n\ge0$ with $t_n=o(n^{2/3})$, $$\mu_J\!\left\{x:
 \left\lVert e^{t_n\mathcal L_J}(x,\cdot)-\mu_J\right\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}>\frac14\right\}
 \longrightarrow1$$ in probability over disorder. For every deterministic nonnegative integer sequence $k_n=o(n^{5/3})$, the same assertion holds with $P_J^{k_n}$. Let $\Sigma_J=\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_{\mu_J}(X)$ and $$R_{\mathrm{lin},J}=\sup_{a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}}
       \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_J}(a^{\mathsf T}X)}{\mathcal D_J(a^{\mathsf T}X)}.$$ For every positive deterministic $M_n\to\infty$, with probability tending to one both $\left\lVert\Sigma_J\right\rVert$ and $R_{\mathrm{lin},J}$ belong to $[n^{2/3}/M_n,M_n n^{2/3}]$.*

</div>

In the realized-start assertion, one samples an initial configuration from $\mu_J$ and holds it fixed before taking the transition law and its TV distance. Averaging that transition law over the initial configuration would instead give $\mu_J$ at every time. The last assertion concerns covariance and linear Rayleigh quotients. Its arbitrary-diverging-factor upper bound does not extend here to the full relaxation or logarithmic Sobolev constant: the upper estimates in [thm:main](#thm:main) have every fixed positive exponent slack. For other fixed TV thresholds below $1/2$, the lower bound in [thm:main](#thm:main) follows by testing the slowest gap eigenfunction, as shown in [sec:dynamics](#sec:dynamics). The realized-start assertion itself retains its stated threshold $1/4$.

The result concerns exactly the critical, zero-field Gaussian model. It gives the mixing exponent and does not assert a cutoff, a cutoff window, or a leading constant. The two upper-bound arguments retain their separate intermediate conclusions and parameter choices.

<a id="pm-h-3"></a>
###### The development of the dynamical question.

Sherrington and Kirkpatrick introduced the infinite-range spin-glass model in 1975 (Sherrington and Kirkpatrick 1975) <a id="pm-cite-2"></a>[[SherringtonKirkpatrick1975](#ref-SherringtonKirkpatrick1975)]. Their later analysis with Gaussian couplings studied single-spin Glauber relaxation through a linearized mean-field calculation and Monte Carlo simulations (Kirkpatrick and Sherrington 1978, sec. VII) <a id="pm-cite-3"></a>[[KirkpatrickSherrington1978](#ref-KirkpatrickSherrington1978)]. A parallel dynamical mean-field program described correlation and response functions in soft-spin Langevin models; the infinite-range specialization was developed by Sompolinsky and Zippelius (Sompolinsky and Zippelius 1982) <a id="pm-cite-4"></a>[[SompolinskyZippelius1982](#ref-SompolinskyZippelius1982)]. These studies examined relaxation near the transition through correlation and response. The finite-size mixing question asks how long the full distribution, started from the most difficult configuration, takes to approach equilibrium.

Numerical work later examined how the critical time scale grows with the number of spins. Billoire’s study of slow samples used binary couplings $J_{ij}=\pm n^{-1/2}$ (Billoire 2011) <a id="pm-cite-5"></a>[[Billoire2011SlowSamples](#ref-Billoire2011SlowSamples)]. Billoire and Campbell’s subsequent critical study measured the equilibrium autocorrelation $q(t)=n^{-1}\sum_i\langle X_i(0)X_i(t)\rangle$ after equilibration. For heat-bath updates, with time measured in updates per spin, it tested the finite-size scaling form $q_c(n,t)\sim n^{-1/3}F(t/n^{2/3})$ (Billoire and Campbell 2011, equation (7)) <a id="pm-cite-6"></a>[[BilloireCampbell2011CriticalDynamics](#ref-BilloireCampbell2011CriticalDynamics)]. That critical preprint does not restate the coupling law. We use its reported collapse as numerical evidence about equilibrium autocorrelation, keeping it separate from the Gaussian worst-start question here.

<a id="pm-h-4"></a>
###### Rigorous high-temperature dynamics.

For comparison with the critical law <a href="#eq:gibbs-law" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:gibbs-law">[eq:gibbs-law]</a>, inverse temperature $\beta$ multiplies its exponent by $\beta$; the resulting interaction entries have variance $\beta^2/n$. The SK statements below hold with high probability over disorder. The inverse temperature $\beta>0$ is fixed inside each stated range, and mixing bounds use fixed total-variation accuracy unless $\varepsilon$ is displayed. Spectral criteria gave functional inequalities well inside the high-temperature phase. Bauerschmidt and Bodineau proved a logarithmic Sobolev inequality under a spectral-width condition that applies to SK for fixed $\beta<1/4$ (Bauerschmidt and Bodineau 2019, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2) <a id="pm-cite-7"></a>[[BauerschmidtBodineau2019](#ref-BauerschmidtBodineau2019)]. For Ising spins their energy is the unweighted full spin-flip gradient. The heat-bath form $\mathcal D_J$ instead retains conditional variance weights, so that result is not the heat-bath inequality used in this paper. Eldan, Koehler, and Zeitouni obtained a heat-bath spectral gap uniform over external fields under the corresponding shifted spectral condition. Their field-dependent worst-start bound gives polynomial mixing for zero-field SK in the range $\beta<1/4$ (Eldan, Koehler, and Zeitouni 2022, Theorems 1 and 11, Section 5) <a id="pm-cite-8"></a>[[EldanKoehlerZeitouni2022](#ref-EldanKoehlerZeitouni2022)]. Anari, Jain, Koehler, Pham, and Vuong then obtained $O_\beta(n\log n)$ random-site attempts in that range, uniformly over external fields, through a modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality (Anari et al. 2021, Theorem 12) <a id="pm-cite-9"></a>[[AnariJainKoehlerPhamVuong2021](#ref-AnariJainKoehlerPhamVuong2021)].

Subsequent work increased the temperature range. Anari, Koehler, and Vuong derived a criterion governed by a Volterra equation; it gives $O(n\log n)$ attempted updates for SK below a reported numerical threshold of approximately $\beta=0.295$ (Anari, Koehler, and Vuong 2024, Theorem 3 and Section 1.3) <a id="pm-cite-10"></a>[[AnariKoehlerVuong2024](#ref-AnariKoehlerVuong2024)]. Wang proved $O_\beta(n\log(n/\varepsilon))$ attempted updates for every fixed $\beta<1/2$, with high probability simultaneously over external fields and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ (Wang 2026, Theorem 1.1) <a id="pm-cite-11"></a>[[Wang2026OptimalMixing](#ref-Wang2026OptimalMixing)]. At zero field, Boban, Li, and Oveis Gharan obtained a constant per-site spectral gap and an $O(n^2)$ attempted-update bound for $\beta<1/2+\varepsilon_0$, with a universal $\varepsilon_0>0$ (Boban, Li, and Oveis Gharan 2026, Theorem 1.5 and Corollary 1.6) <a id="pm-cite-12"></a>[[BobanLiOveisGharan2026](#ref-BobanLiOveisGharan2026)]. The companion spectral-gap theorem covers each fixed zero-field $0<\beta<1$, with a constant that may depend on $\beta$ (OpenAI 2026a, Theorem 1.1) <a id="pm-cite-13"></a>[[AcceptedGap](#ref-AcceptedGap)]. None of these fixed-subcritical bounds supplies a bound at $\beta=1$ by taking a limit. At that endpoint the critical companion identifies the slow linear and realized-start scales in [thm:accepted-critical](#thm:accepted-critical); the present upper bounds match their exponents for the full dynamics.

<a id="pm-h-5"></a>
###### Static comparisons and the two critical mechanisms.

The equilibrium geometry behind the critical scale is accessible through comparison with spins on a sphere. Comets conditioned on the eigenvalues of a GOE completion and averaged its eigenframe, obtaining an exact conditional first-moment identity between cube and spherical partition functions (Comets 1996, equations (2.1)–(2.2)) <a id="pm-cite-14"></a>[[Comets1996Spherical](#ref-Comets1996Spherical)]. At criticality, Du and Huang developed sharper comparisons for free energy and overlap. Their local overlap-cell estimates compare partition-function moments (Du and Huang 2026a, Theorem 1.6 and Section 3.3) <a id="pm-cite-15"></a>[[DuHuang2026CriticalFluctuations](#ref-DuHuang2026CriticalFluctuations)], and their mixed cube–sphere tensor calculation cancels leading terms in a squared norm (Du and Huang 2026b, sec. 3.2, Lemma 3.5) <a id="pm-cite-16"></a>[[DuHuang2026CriticalOverlap](#ref-DuHuang2026CriticalOverlap)]. These are static comparisons. The upper bounds here need corresponding control after observations have changed the field and interaction, together with probability estimates strong enough for arbitrary test functions.

Gaussian stochastic localization supplies the framework for revealing those observations while tracking the remaining variance or entropy (Eldan 2013; Chen and Eldan 2025) <a id="pm-cite-17"></a>[[Eldan2013StochasticLocalization](#ref-Eldan2013StochasticLocalization), [ChenEldan2025Localization](#ref-ChenEldan2025Localization)]. The root calculation also develops conditional Kac–Rice methods used for TAP landscapes by Fan, Mei, and Montanari, and by Celentano, Fan, and Mei (Fan, Mei, and Montanari 2021; Celentano, Fan, and Mei 2023) <a id="pm-cite-18"></a>[[FanMeiMontanari2021](#ref-FanMeiMontanari2021), [CelentanoFanMei2023](#ref-CelentanoFanMei2023)]. Their cited applications have different positive-overlap or fixed-signal hypotheses; the shrinking-overlap critical estimates are proved here. The isotropic route extends the signed spin–Gaussian comparison to observation-dependent fields, then improves a typical-orientation estimate along the observation path. The cap route keeps the reduction of covariance in the field direction while fresh rotations reduce errors in orthogonal directions inside the active spectral subspace. The entropy arguments use these estimates only on their stated path or field domains and pay for their exceptions. [sec:proof-overview](#sec:proof-overview) describes the inputs and outputs of the two mechanisms in detail.

<a id="sec:model"></a>
### Conventions and Gaussian observations

For a full-support law $\nu$ on $\Omega_n$, we write $$\mathcal D_\nu(f)=\sum_i\nu\!\left[\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\nu(f\mid X_{-i})\right].$$ Conditional expectation given all spins except one is an orthogonal projection on $L^2(\nu)$. The average of these projections therefore has spectrum in $[0,1]$. Its Dirichlet form is $\mathcal D_\nu/n$, a fact used later to pass directly from continuous time to deterministic numbers of attempted updates. For $f(x)=a^{\mathsf T}x$, <a id="eq:linear-energy"></a>$$\label{eq:linear-energy}
 \mathcal D_\nu(f)=\sum_i a_i^2\nu\!\left[\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\nu(X_i\mid X_{-i})\right]
 \le\left\lVert a\right\rVert^2.$$ All vector norms are Euclidean and all matrix norms are operator norms unless another norm is indicated. Empirical averages have a factor $1/n$.

We use the orthogonal invariance of a GOE completion. Adjoin independent $J_{ii}\sim N(0,2/n)$ to $J^\circ$ and call the completed matrix $J$. The added energy is $\frac12\sum_iJ_{ii}$ because $x_i^2=1$; it is constant on the cube. Hence the Gibbs law, transition kernels, and all functional constants are unchanged. We may condition on the eigenvalues of $J$ and use its Haar-distributed eigenframe in intermediate estimates. Once the conclusion is expressed in these intrinsic quantities, it is a statement about the original off-diagonal disorder.

For matrix $A$ and field $h$, a tilted spin law is proportional to $\exp(x^{\mathsf T}Ax/2+h^{\mathsf T}x)$. A Gaussian observation of positive semidefinite precision $B$ has value $$Y=BX+B^{1/2}G,$$ where $G$ is standard Gaussian independent of $X$. Expanding the Gaussian likelihood shows that the posterior adds $Y$ to the field and subtracts $B$ from the interaction. Density calculations take place on the range of $B$; null directions carry no observation. In the isotropic case $B=sI$, the subtraction is diagonal and the posterior is simply a field tilt of the original spin law. Spectral caps use the same identity with a matrix precision.

<a id="eq:common-energy-contraction"></a>
For increasing deterministic precisions, independent Gaussian increments give the same experiment. At time $s$ let $\mu_s$ be the posterior law, $m_s=\mu_s X$ and $\Sigma_s=\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_{\mu_s}(X)$. The isotropic experiment is $Y_s=sX+B_s$, with $B_s$ standard Brownian motion. Its innovation $I_s:=Y_s-\int_0^s m_u\,\mathrm du$ is Brownian in the observation filtration. The finite-prior filtering identity is <a id="eq:common-filtering"></a>$$\label{eq:common-filtering}
 \mathrm d(\mu_s f)=\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_{\mu_s}(f,X)^{\mathsf T}\mathrm dI_s.$$ Conditioning also gives $$\label{eq:common-energy-contraction}
 \mathbb E\mathcal D_{\mu_s}(f)\le\mathcal D_{\mu_0}(f).$$ This is the finite-prior form of Gaussian stochastic localization (Eldan 2013) <a id="pm-cite-19"></a>[[Eldan2013StochasticLocalization](#ref-Eldan2013StochasticLocalization)]. The posterior formula is given in (Chen and Eldan 2025, sec. 2.4.2, Fact 14 and Equation (6), arXiv version 2) <a id="pm-cite-20"></a>[[ChenEldan2025Localization](#ref-ChenEldan2025Localization)]; the entropy drift and associated stability criteria appear in its Equation (27), Proposition 39 and Lemma 40. The contraction <a href="#eq:common-energy-contraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:common-energy-contraction">[eq:common-energy-contraction]</a> is the heat-bath Dirichlet-form supermartingale of (Eldan, Koehler, and Zeitouni 2022, Lemma 9, arXiv version 2) <a id="pm-cite-21"></a>[[EldanKoehlerZeitouni2022](#ref-EldanKoehlerZeitouni2022)]. The gap companion records these temperature-free identities with the same normalization (OpenAI 2026a, sec. 2) <a id="pm-cite-22"></a>[[AcceptedGap](#ref-AcceptedGap)].

The critical task is to bound the posterior quantities in these identities on the observation paths actually used. Each route proves those estimates, including the cost of exceptional observations. In particular, a covariance estimate on one random path is not an all-tilts stability theorem, and the classical logarithmic Sobolev inequality will require its own entropy and layer argument.

For a nonnegative density $g$ with $\mu g=1$, $\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(g\mu\Vert\mu)
=\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(g)$. The classical inequality studied here is $\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(f^2)\le C_{\mathrm{LS}}\mathcal D_\mu(f)$ for all real $f$. Here the energy acts on $f$, while the entropy acts on $f^2$. An estimate using the logarithmic entropy-production form of $g$ would be a different inequality and does not replace this one. For a fixed law on the finite cube every real function is admissible. Unless a varying parameter is explicitly specified, all constants and tolerances are chosen before $n$ tends to infinity.

<a id="sec:accepted-inputs"></a>
### Companion inputs and the critical endpoint

The critical companion supplies exactly the two statements collected in [thm:accepted-critical](#thm:accepted-critical): its Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 (OpenAI 2026b) <a id="pm-cite-23"></a>[[AcceptedCritical](#ref-AcceptedCritical)]. The spectral, noncentral spherical, and spectral-cap estimates required by the upper bounds are proved below. The high-temperature gap companion supplies observation identities and deterministic field and residual tools, together with fixed-subcritical consequences under their stated hypotheses (OpenAI 2026a) <a id="pm-cite-24"></a>[[AcceptedGap](#ref-AcceptedGap)]. We describe these hypotheses before using the tools at a critical endpoint.

The field equations are of Thouless–Anderson–Palmer type (Thouless, Anderson, and Palmer 1977) <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[TAP1977](#ref-TAP1977)]. We use the following normalization, including the rank-one derivative of the self-consistent overlap.

For an interaction of variance $j/n$, set $$\begin{aligned}
 m&=\tanh y,&q&=n^{-1}\left\lVert m\right\rVert^2,&V_y&=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(1-m_i^2),\\
 F_{J,h}(y)&=y-h+[j(1-q)I-J]m,&&&\\
 H_J(y,A)&=I+A^{1/2}
       [j(1-q)I-J-2jmm^{\mathsf T}/n]A^{1/2}.&&&
\end{aligned}$$ The stable-field hypothesis is uniform over a region: every $y$ with $\left\lVert F_{J,h}(y)\right\rVert\le\rho_0\sqrt n$ and every diagonal $0\le A\le(1+\eta)I$ sufficiently close to $V_y$ in normalized Frobenius norm must satisfy $H_J(y,A)\succ cI$. The constants $\rho_0,\eta,c$ are fixed positive margins. The whole-region assertion permits root continuation and spin-flip buffers; positivity at one selected root would not supply these uses.

The matrix diagnostics used below concern finite *words*: ordered products of bounded diagonal matrices and copies of the interaction matrix, with at most one controlled inverse factor. They bound the operator norm, the entrywise $\ell^4$ norm off the diagonal, and the Euclidean norm of the diagonal error from its Gaussian contraction prediction. The permitted diagonal classes and the actual inverse margins are stated in [prof:endpoint-words](#prof:endpoint-words), [cap:restricted-words](#cap:restricted-words); the distinction between adaptive diagonals and prescribed vector tests is recorded below.

<a id="pm-h-8"></a>
###### Deterministic consequences.

Under the specified finite-word diagnostics and stable-field hypotheses, the root $r$ is unique. The gap paper’s Proposition 7.2 gives <a id="eq:accepted-directional"></a>$$\label{eq:accepted-directional}
 \left\lVert\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_{\mu_h}(G,X)\right\rVert
 \le C\bigl(\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_h}(G)+\mathcal D_{\mu_h}(G)\bigr)^{1/2}.$$ Its proof also establishes $|\mu_h[G(X-\tanh r)^{\mathsf T}e]|
\le C(\mu_h G^2+\mathcal D_{\mu_h}(G))^{1/2}$ for $\left\lVert e\right\rVert\le1$. In particular, <a id="eq:accepted-ordinary-mean"></a>$$\label{eq:accepted-ordinary-mean}
 \left\lVert\mu_hX-\tanh r\right\rVert\le C.$$ This is an unnormalized Euclidean mean estimate; it is not an approximation for the derivative of the mean map. For $N=\mu_h f^2>0$ and $\nu=f^2\mu_h/N$, Proposition 7.3 gives, for each sufficiently small fixed $\delta>0$, <a id="eq:accepted-weighted-mean"></a>$$\label{eq:accepted-weighted-mean}
 \frac{\left\lVert\nu X-\tanh r\right\rVert}{\sqrt n}
 \le C\delta+\frac{C_\delta}{\sqrt n}
                 \left(1+\frac{\mathcal D_{\mu_h}(f)}N\right).$$ The leading constant $C$ is fixed by the stability margins. The constant $C_\delta$ and the finite diagnostic length may then depend on $\delta$ and on the resulting residual-recipe depth. This distinction will matter when we choose an integrated entropy-drift budget before choosing the residual tolerance that realizes it. The displayed statements and the uncentered proof consequence come from (OpenAI 2026a, sec. 6, Lemma 7.1, Proposition 7.2 and its proof, Proposition 7.3) <a id="pm-cite-26"></a>[[AcceptedGap](#ref-AcceptedGap)].

<a id="pm-h-9"></a>
###### Provider hypotheses.

In the provider’s random word estimates, $j<1$ and $j(1+\eta)^2<1$ are fixed. When the interaction is $\beta$ times a standard SK matrix, this variance parameter is $j=\beta^2$. Words have fixed length and at most one inverse factor; that inverse requires a separate positive margin for the actual matrix being inverted. Bilinear estimates apply to prescribed finite families of deterministic vectors. The random stable-field theorem is along ordinary Gaussian observations of a zero-field Gibbs sample. It is not a theorem for every field. The terminal observation-gap theorem also fixes $j<1$, although its input spin law may be arbitrary (OpenAI 2026a, Proposition 5.1, Corollary 5.2, Proposition 8.3) <a id="pm-cite-27"></a>[[AcceptedGap](#ref-AcceptedGap)].

Some deterministic ingredients have broader domains. The root/inverse lemma permits every fixed $j>0$ provided $H_J(y,V_y)\succeq cI$ throughout its entire small-residual region. That root lemma alone needs only $A=V_y$; the nearby-diagonal condition is an additional hypothesis for the implicit residual recipes. The local-volume lemma and the signed two-spin curvature inequality similarly have their explicit deterministic hypotheses (OpenAI 2026a, Lemmas 5.6, 5.7 and 8.1) <a id="pm-cite-28"></a>[[AcceptedGap](#ref-AcceptedGap)]. We apply these deterministic tools at $j=1$ only after verifying their hypotheses. The two routes prove the needed restricted norm–trace random diagnostics, actual adaptive-inverse margins, whole-region stability, and terminal extensions locally. Recipe depth is fixed before the number of allowed spin flips, buffer widths, and eventual large-$n$ threshold are used. No critical random estimate is obtained by taking $\beta\uparrow1$ in the fixed-temperature spectral-gap theorem.

<a id="sec:proof-overview"></a>
### Two upper-bound mechanisms

Both proofs use the geometry of the upper spectral edge, but transport different estimates. The limiting GOE spectral density decays as the square root of the distance to its upper edge $2$, making $nu^{3/2}$ the characteristic dimension of an edge window of width $u$. The spectral estimates below make this count precise at the scales where it is used. A spherical spin law can be represented as a Gaussian conditioned on $\|X\|^2=n$, so its resolvent turns this edge geometry into explicit covariance estimates. The first route observes all directions at the same precision. The second observes only the soft edge directions and enlarges that set one spectral cap at a time.

All changes of law below use finite-dimensional likelihood identities with explicit partition normalizers. The planted law weights the disorder by its partition function and introduces an auxiliary spin. Estimates under that law, or under a further tilt, are returned to ordinary disorder with the stated probability cost. No critical contiguity assertion is used; the distinction at the spiked-Wigner threshold is discussed in (Perry et al. 2018, Appendix A) <a id="pm-cite-29"></a>[[PerryWeinBandeiraMoitra2018](#ref-PerryWeinBandeiraMoitra2018)].

<a id="pm-h-11"></a>
#### Isotropic observations: from covariance to a support profile

The endpoint of the first route is [prof:support-profile](#prof:support-profile): for every fixed $\omega>0$, on one disorder event of probability tending to one, $$\mathcal D_J(f)\ge c_\omega n^{-2/3-\omega}\log(1/p)\,\mu_J(f^2),
 \qquad 0<p:=\mu_J(f\ne0)\le\tfrac12,$$ simultaneously for every nonzero real $f$. The factor $\log(1/p)$ says that a function concentrated on a smaller set must pay more heat-bath energy relative to its squared norm. For an indicator, $\mathcal D_J(\mathbf1_A)=\sum_{x\in A}\mu_J(x)\sum_iQ_i(x,A^c)$ is the stationary probability current out of $A$ per unit of per-site time. The profile controls the early evolution of a point-start density; the spectral gap controls the final decay.

<a id="pm-h-12"></a>
###### A local covariance comparison.

At isotropic precision $s$, write $r=\sqrt s$ and $k=nr^3=ns^{3/2}$. The spectral and spherical estimates in [prof:sec:spectral](#prof:sec:spectral) locate the Gaussian saddle and control its length densities, projections, and replica overlaps. The unrestricted rotation comparison in [prof:sec:unconstrained](#prof:sec:unconstrained) then compares the spin and spherical partition functions and their replica moments. These estimates give the continuous reference and the probability budgets for the root analysis.

The root analysis studies solutions of $$y+(1-q)m-Jm=h_s,\qquad m=\tanh y,\qquad q=n^{-1}\|m\|^2.$$ The Kac–Rice formula in [prof:roots](#prof:roots) expresses planted expectations of sums over regular solutions as an integral against the observation density and the absolute Jacobian determinant. After gauging the planted spin to $\mathbf1$, the conditional matrix calculation in [prof:matrices](#prof:matrices) isolates three directions: $m$; the component of $\mathbf1$ orthogonal to $m$; and the component of the root field $y$ orthogonal to both. Their span is $\mathcal P$. The last direction records the remaining cubic part of the root profile. Conditioning on these directions leaves Haar rotations on $\mathcal P^\perp$. [prof:orbits](#prof:orbits) compares their Haar weights with the determinant weights in the root count and locates the Gaussian trace. The exclusions are integrated over the root and conditional matrix data, with the imposed spectral restriction. The degree-one argument controls multiplicity when this root count is returned to the planted field law.

Here is the cancellation at the center of the comparison. Put $z=X-m$. For each replica, fix its projection on $\mathcal P$ and its translated length; for a pair, also record the overlap of their residual components in $\mathcal P^\perp$. The two replica types are a product spin prior with means $m$ and a variable-variance Gaussian prior. Multiplication by the common quadratic weight $\exp\{z^{\mathsf T}(J-(1-q)I)z/2\}$ turns the product spin prior into the posterior $\mu_s$ in the translated coordinates: the root equation cancels its linear term. The quantities $\mathcal R_{ij}$ in <a href="#prof:eq16" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prof:eq16">[prof:eq16]</a> are their conditional saddle-density ratios for this residual overlap, relative to a common continuous reference, for the four ordered type pairs. A projection multiplier first matches the one-replica saddle densities. The signed combination $\mathcal R_{pp}-\mathcal R_{pg_0}-\mathcal R_{g_0p}
+\mathcal R_{g_0g_0}$, with the common projection weight in <a href="#prof:eq16" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prof:eq16">[prof:eq16]</a>, cancels common errors and errors depending on only one replica type. The actual spin statistics retain their lattice measures: [prof:common-angular-kernel](#prof:common-angular-kernel), [prof:mixed-coordinate-transfer](#prof:mixed-coordinate-transfer) transfer only the smooth leading terms to common volume, after bounding each remainder on its own measure.

This signed estimate, including the centered matrix kernel of [prof:gaussian-signed-kernel](#prof:gaussian-signed-kernel), yields [prof:median-covariance](#prof:median-covariance). For $k\ge\log^{10}n$ and sufficiently small $r$, most Haar orientations on each retained root orbit satisfy $\|\Sigma_s\|\le(1+\epsilon)/s$, together with the weighted covariance and mean bounds in <a href="#prof:eq13" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="prof:eq13">[prof:eq13]</a>. Those additional bounds control derivatives along rotations in the next stage.

<a id="pm-h-13"></a>
###### A probability bound along the observation path.

[prof:prop-amplified-covariance](#prof:prop-amplified-covariance) combines short backward variance transfers with concentration around the local majority just obtained. Starting from fixed positive observation times, it bounds, at each deterministic time with $0<s\le s_0$ and $k\ge K_{\log}\log n$, the integrated planted mass of $\mathcal G\cap\{\|\Sigma_s\|>(1+\epsilon)/s\}$ by $e^{-ak}$. Here $\mathcal G$ is the rotation-invariant good-spectrum event in the proposition. The positive-time covariance and terminal gap inputs are proved at the critical parameter in [prof:positive-inputs](#prof:positive-inputs); the subcritical spectral-gap theorem is not applied at its endpoint. In the intervening polylogarithmic window, the induction uses the unrestricted comparison of [prof:sec:polylog](#prof:sec:polylog) in place of root-preserving rotations.

For the bottom range, put $\ell=\log\log(n+1000)$. At each deterministic time with $k\le K_{\log}\log n$, [prof:prop-bottom-covariance](#prof:prop-bottom-covariance) bounds the integrated planted mass of $\mathcal G\cap\{\|\Sigma_s\|>Cn^{2/3}\ell^C\}$ by $n^{-B}$ for any fixed $B>0$. Its finite-replica expansion retains the central prefactors and lattice covolumes. After conversion to common volume, the alternating sum cancels every term that omits a replica label; increasing the fixed moment order then supplies the required probability exponent. These are estimates along the observation law at deterministic times, with their stated integrated exceptions.

<a id="pm-h-14"></a>
###### Entropy and the uniform event.

[prof:entropy](#prof:entropy) first transfers the planted bounds to one typical ordinary-disorder event, before choosing $f$. After normalizing $\mu_J(f^2)=1$, the restricted step assumes $0<p:=\mu_J(f\ne0)\le1/2$ and $\|f\|_\infty^2\le100p^{-2}$. It treats small, moderate, and order-$n$ values of $\log(1/p)$ separately. Variance transport uses the bottom-scale estimate in the first range; replica moments and the sharp covariance bound retain entropy in the second; square-reweighted mean estimates control the last range. The product endpoint converts retained entropy to heat-bath energy, giving [prof:restricted-profile](#prof:restricted-profile). Dyadic layers remove the bounded-test restriction and prove the support profile stated above.

<a id="pm-h-15"></a>
#### Spectral caps: from a radial deficit to log-Sobolev

The second route proves [cap:thm-lsi](#cap:thm-lsi): for every fixed $\rho>0$, with probability tending to one, $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mu_J}(f^2)\le n^{2/3+\rho}\mathcal D_J(f)
 \qquad\text{for every real }f.$$ This classical logarithmic Sobolev inequality controls the smoothing of arbitrary densities through hypercontractivity and also implies the Poincaré inequality.

<a id="pm-h-16"></a>
###### The cap and the radial deficit.

Let $d=2I-J$. At scale $p$, observe with precision $B_p=(p^2-d)_+$ and write $J_p=J-B_p$. On the spectral event used below, the active projection $P_p=\mathbf1_{\{d\le p^2\}}$ has rank of order $k_p=np^3$; the cap makes $J_p$ scalar on its range. For $h$ in this range, the spherical comparison uses $R_p=(\max(d,p^2)+\alpha)^{-1}$, where $\alpha$ is chosen so that $\operatorname{Tr}R_p+\|R_ph\|^2=n$. [cap:static-comparison](#cap:static-comparison) controls partition values and projected means uniformly on each prescribed ball $\|h\|\le R p^2M_p$, where $M_p=\sqrt{np}$ and $R$ is fixed.

Changing the field radially changes the length of the Gaussian mean, so the sphere constraint also changes $\alpha$. This reduces the radial response relative to the frozen resolvent $R_p$. The induction records that reduction explicitly. The true potential is $\phi_p(h)=\log Z_{J_p}(h)$, whose Hessian is the capped Gibbs covariance. For this potential, $K_p=(P_p\nabla^2\phi_p(h)P_p)|_{\operatorname{ran}P_p}$. During initialization, $K_p$ instead denotes the Hessian of an auxiliary potential on the same space. Restrict $R_p$ there as well. With $e=h/\|h\|$, on the prescribed annulus the matrix $D=p^2(K_p-R_p)$ has a radial entry at most $-0.30$, small transverse and mixed blocks, and a bounded lower error; see <a href="#cap:invariant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cap:invariant">[cap:invariant]</a>. This negative radial correction is the *radial deficit*. It provides the gain needed to propagate the covariance estimate to a smaller cap.

<a id="pm-h-17"></a>
###### Transport and initialization.

The curvature induction proceeds from larger caps to smaller caps. After the estimates have been proved, the entropy argument uses them along the forward observation process, in which $p$ and $B_p$ increase. For a child scale $c=\gamma p$, the exact Gaussian convolution <a href="#cap:heat-convolution" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cap:heat-convolution">[cap:heat-convolution]</a> expresses the child potential through the parent. The exact increment formula conjugates the covariance of the parent field under the transition law by the inverse precision increment, then subtracts that inverse increment, to obtain the child’s Hessian. The Brascamp–Lieb upper bound retains the radial correction through the inverse in <a href="#cap:bl-recursion" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cap:bl-recursion">[cap:bl-recursion]</a>; the variational Fisher lower bound controls the opposite side and the mixed block. Averaging the rank-one correction regenerates the radial deficit by <a href="#cap:radial-regeneration" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cap:radial-regeneration">[cap:radial-regeneration]</a>. Meanwhile the still hidden eigenframe inside the flat parent space is Haar. Its compression makes the transverse error small enough at the child scale. This conditional rotation is used under the canonical Gaussian bridge before the change to the actual tilted transition. [cap:curvature-induction](#cap:curvature-induction) is the resulting one-step statement.

The initial radial deficit comes from the small-field TAP expansion in [cap:classical](#cap:classical), specifically [cap:tap-expansion](#cap:tap-expansion). [cap:auxiliary-initialization](#cap:auxiliary-initialization) uses an independent conditional completion of the first cap to construct an auxiliary potential with the curvature invariant and a bounded Euclidean gradient error from the true potential. The companion estimate used for that error is at one fixed $0<\beta<1$. [cap:gradient-contraction](#cap:gradient-contraction) contracts the error over a finite number of cap steps, and [cap:remove-auxiliary](#cap:remove-auxiliary) then transfers the invariant to the true potential. The induction continues down to $np^3\asymp\sqrt{\log n}$. For fields $h\in\operatorname{ran}P_p$, its final output, [cap:true-curvature](#cap:true-curvature), gives a sharp $(1+\epsilon)/p^2$ upper bound for the covariance projected onto $\operatorname{ran}P_p$ on a thin saddle annulus, and a $C/p^2$ bound for the same projected covariance on any prescribed bounded field ball, at every scale in the stated interval.

<a id="pm-h-18"></a>
###### Entropy retention and layers.

Write $N=\mu_J(f^2)=e^{-L}>0$ and $\nu=f^2\mu_J/N$. The bounded-test reduction assumes $0\le f\le1$, $\mu_J(f>0)\le1/2$, $\operatorname{KL}(\nu\Vert\mu_J)\ge L/2$, and $L\le Cn$. The disorder event is chosen before $f$. For $L\le\lambda n$, where the small fixed $\lambda>0$ is chosen after the curvature and ordinary-path tolerances, [cap:entropy-retention](#cap:entropy-retention) chooses a first cap with dimension comparable to $\max\{\sqrt{\log n},c_0L\}$. The curvature bounds control the information revealed as the cap grows, retaining enough entropy for the product estimate in [cap:product-estimate](#cap:product-estimate). For $\lambda n\le L\le Cn$, [cap:large-entropy](#cap:large-entropy) argues by contradiction under $\mathcal D_J(f)/N\le n^{-2/3}L$. Square-reweighted mean bounds and relative entropy of stopped observation paths retain order-$n$ entropy until the product estimate contradicts that assumption. The noise diagnostics and stability tolerances are chosen before the test function. Finally, [cap:layer-lemma](#cap:layer-lemma) passes from the bounded-test energy estimate to set capacities, then to arbitrary half-supported functions, and then by a median decomposition and the entropy shift <a href="#cap:entropy-shift" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cap:entropy-shift">[cap:entropy-shift]</a> to the classical logarithmic Sobolev inequality.

<a id="pm-h-19"></a>
###### The final dynamical transfer.

[sec:dynamics](#sec:dynamics) converts either functional endpoint to worst-start mixing: the support profile truncates large densities, while logarithmic Sobolev hypercontractivity supplies the second smoothing argument. The identity $\mathcal L_J=n(P_J-I)$ and the nonnegative spectrum of $P_J$ keep the factor $n$ between per-site time and attempted updates explicit. The linear lower tests and [thm:accepted-critical](#thm:accepted-critical) supply the opposite exponents for mixing and the functional constants. The companion’s realized-start and arbitrary-diverging-factor quantifiers remain those stated in [thm:accepted-critical](#thm:accepted-critical).

<a id="prof:sec:spectral"></a>
### Spectral and spherical estimates for the support-profile argument

The support-profile argument begins with estimates that involve only the spectrum and unrestricted rotation orbits. These estimates have two uses. At positive observation times they provide fixed-rate overlap concentration and exponential-moment bounds with arbitrarily prescribed exceptional-set rates. At the smallest times a more accurate comparison with the spherical model gives covariance estimates and an independent lower-bound argument.

<a id="prof:subsec:conventions"></a>
#### Conventions and the observation law

The matrix $J$ has the GOE normalization: its independent off-diagonal entries have variance $1/n$, and its diagonal entries have variance $2/n$. The diagonal does not affect the spin law. Write $\pi_{\mathrm c}$ for uniform probability measure on $\{-1,1\}^n$, and $\pi_{\mathrm o}$ for uniform probability measure on the sphere of radius $\sqrt n$. Define $$Z(h)=\int \exp\{x^TJx/2+h^Tx\}\,\mathrm d\pi_{\mathrm c}(x),
 \qquad
 Z_{\mathrm o}(h)=\int \exp\{x^TJx/2+h^Tx\}\,\mathrm d\pi_{\mathrm o}(x).$$ Thus the partition functions use probability, rather than counting or surface-area, normalization. The spin law at field $h$ is $\mu_h$. Empirical averages are denoted by $\left\langle a\right\rangle=n^{-1}\sum_i a_i$; vector norms are Euclidean, matrix norms without a subscript are operator norms, and $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$ is the Hilbert–Schmidt norm.

Given $J$, sample $X$ from $\mu_0$ and observe $$h_s=sX+B_s,\qquad r=\sqrt s,\qquad k=nr^3,$$ where $B$ is an independent standard Brownian motion in $\mathbb R^n$. Completing the square in the Gaussian likelihood shows that the conditional spin law is $\mu_s:=\mu_{h_s}$. Its mean and covariance will be denoted by $m_s^{\mathrm{post}}$ and $\Sigma_s$, respectively.

There are two probability laws for the disorder. The ordinary law is the centered GOE law. The planted law is its size bias by $Z(0)/\mathbb EZ(0)$, together with the Gibbs spin and observation. Under the present normalization $\mathbb EZ(0)=e^{n/4}$. Under the planted law, $X$ is uniform on the cube and $$J=W+XX^T/n,$$ where $W$ is an independent centered GOE matrix. This follows directly by completing squares in its Gaussian density. A second exact identity will be used repeatedly.
